lines.name: BART Silicon Valley Phase II
lines.summary: VTA's six-mile extension of BART from Berryessa through downtown San José to Santa Clara, with three underground stations, one at-grade station and a rail yard, built around a single tunnel about 53 feet across. Its adopted budget is $12.7 billion. Early works are under way at the tunnel launch site, but the federal grant that would pay for about 40% of it is not yet signed, and service is scheduled for 2039 (VTA aims for 2037).

lines.notes: Status translated from BAM's stage (infrastructure): BAM stage 'infrastructure': early construction ahead of tunneling (launch structure dug, demolition and utility relocation at station sites). Stage note at 2026-10-07: Early construction, ahead of tunneling. Crews finished excavating the West Portal launch structure for the tunnel boring machine in early September 2026, and demolition and utility relocation are under way at station sites. In August 2026 VTA signed a restated tunnel contract and gave notice to proceed with pre-tunneling work only. The federal grant agreement that would fund most of the line is not yet signed (VTA's target is late 2027), the boring machine is in storage in Germany with delivery expected in the second half of 2027, and FTA's oversight consultant rates the project high risk while VTA re-baselines its cost and schedule.

lines.name: California High-Speed Rail: San Francisco to San Jose
lines.summary: The Bay Area end of California's high-speed rail line. Rather than building new tracks up the Peninsula, high-speed trains would share Caltrain's newly electrified corridor for about 49 miles from San Francisco to San Jose, stopping at Fourth and King (and later the Salesforce Transit Center via The Portal), Millbrae for SFO, and San Jose Diridon. The route was environmentally approved in 2022, but no construction has started and the Authority's current plan reaches the Bay Area by 2039.

lines.notes: Status translated from BAM's stage (entitled): BAM stage 'entitled': environmentally cleared (ROD Oct 2022); right-of-way, design and station work not started. Stage note at 2026-10-07: Environmentally cleared: the Authority's Board certified the Final EIR/EIS and approved the route in August 2022, and the Record of Decision followed in October 2022. No construction has started. The 2026 Business Plan's schedule lists right-of-way, design, and the Fourth and King, Millbrae and San Jose station work as 'not started'. It plans for trains to reach the Bay Area over upgraded shared tracks by 2039 in its San Francisco–Bakersfield scenario. That depends on funding and on agreements with Caltrain and partners, including for the San Jose to Gilroy line. Until The Portal is built, Fourth and King is the interim terminus.

lines.name: SMART Cloverdale extension
lines.summary: The last leg of the voter-approved SMART system: about 13.5 miles of out-of-service railroad from north of Healdsburg to Cloverdale, with new stations at Geyserville (adopted in August 2026) and Cloverdale. It was environmentally cleared with the rest of the line and is in the regional plan, but it has no construction funding yet.

links.label: Project record in the megaprojects map

lines.notes: Status translated from BAM's stage (proposed): BAM stage 'proposed': environmentally cleared but not yet fully funded, with no construction schedule. Stage note at 2026-10-08: Shown as proposed: environmentally cleared but not yet fully funded, with no construction schedule; SMART says the Cloverdale station will be completed when funding becomes available. SMART's 2006 EIR and 2008 SEIR covered the whole 70-mile corridor to Cloverdale. On Aug 19, 2026 the Board adopted a Geyserville station into SMART's program and approved it as a station project of its own, statutorily exempt from CEQA as a passenger rail project (Public Resources Code 21080.25, as amended by SB 71), to be advanced as part of the extension to Cloverdale; SMART filed the notice of exemption the next day. The extension is in Plan Bay Area 2050+, adopted in March 2026, with a $353 million capital cost and a 2025-2035 opening period, but SMART says it still needs state and federal grants and has applications pending or in development. SMART puts Healdsburg to Cloverdale at about 18 miles, and a Geyserville station at about the midpoint lets it split that into two smaller projects that may compete better for grants. The Cloverdale station site is listed as to be determined, and the Healdsburg design-build contract includes options to continue north if more grants are secured.

lines.name: SMART Healdsburg extension
lines.summary: The next step north for SMART's trains: about nine miles of railroad, idle for decades, rebuilt from today's end of the line at Windsor through Healdsburg, with a new Healdsburg station, a replacement Russian River rail bridge and the SMART Pathway alongside. It is funded at about $269 million, in design, and planned to open in late 2028; where the Healdsburg station goes is being reconsidered.

links.label: Project record in the megaprojects map

lines.notes: Status translated from BAM's stage (entitled): BAM stage 'entitled': funded, environmentally cleared and in design; construction hasn't started. Stage note at 2026-10-08: Funded, environmentally cleared and in design; construction hasn't started. The route is covered by SMART's 2006 EIR and 2008 SEIR for the 70-mile system; the Board adopted an addendum for this segment on Dec 17, 2025, and the California Transportation Commission, as a responsible agency, accepted it and approved the project for future consideration of funding on Jan 29, 2026. The progressive design-build team, under contract since September 2025, had prepared 50% design documents by September 2026, and utility potholing began in April 2026. The first construction package, Windsor Station to Front Street, is due for award in October 2026, with construction starting in spring 2027; a second package, Front Street to North Street, includes the station. SMART is also asking the public where the Healdsburg station should go: the historic Depot/Hudson Street site the City prefers (reaffirmed in September 2026), or a Downtown site on Vine Street about 0.45 mile away. Service is planned for December 2028.

lines.name: The Portal (Downtown Rail Extension)
lines.summary: A rail tunnel to bring Caltrain, and later high-speed rail, from the Fourth and King terminus about 1.3 miles into the Salesforce Transit Center, whose two-level underground train box was built for it and has stood empty since 2018. It adds an underground station at Fourth and Townsend. The $8.3 billion project is environmentally cleared and in federal engineering review, with a $3.38 billion federal grant in sight. It still needs the rest of its local and state funding, and TJPA forecasts service in late 2036.

lines.notes: Status translated from BAM's stage (entitled): BAM stage 'entitled': environmentally cleared, in FTA's Engineering phase, not under construction or fully funded. Stage note at 2026-10-07: Environmentally cleared and in the Engineering phase of FTA's Capital Investment Grants program since May 2024, but not yet under construction or fully funded. Design is at 30% for the tunnel and stations and 60% for the early works. Right-of-way appraisals are under way, and proposals for the civil and tunnel progressive design-build contract are due Oct 9, 2026. The Full Funding Grant Agreement is targeted for July 2027. TJPA says utility relocation construction will start in 2028 and forecasts that the line will be ready for service on Nov 17, 2036.

lines.name: Valley Link
lines.summary: A new passenger rail line along the I-580 corridor linking BART at Dublin/Pleasanton with ACE commuter trains at Vasco Road in Livermore, so riders from the San Joaquin Valley can change trains across a platform instead of driving over the Altamont Pass. The first 11 miles, with three stations and battery-electric trains, are environmentally cleared and in design; an extension to Mountain House is cleared but unfunded.

Stage note at 2026-10-07: Environmentally cleared and in design; no construction yet. The Authority certified the Subsequent EIR for the 22-mile Phase 1 in October 2024 and FTA issued a FONSI on May 27, 2025. In June 2025 the Board split delivery after cost increases at 30% design, starting with the 11-mile Phase 1A to Vasco Road; a joint CEQA addendum and NEPA re-evaluation for the 1.5-mile connection from I-580/First Street to Vasco Road is targeted for fall 2026. A CM/GC preconstruction contract went to Kiewit in June 2026. Construction funding is not yet secured: the Authority is preparing to ask FTA to enter the Capital Investment Grants Engineering phase.

lines.name: Berkeley line

operators.name: Key System (the San Francisco, Oakland & San Jose Railway and its successors)

lines.summary: The Key Route's first line, from its pier to downtown Berkeley by Adeline Street and Shattuck Avenue; cut back to Alcatraz Avenue in 1933, then from 1941 over the Southern Pacific's old tracks to Northbrae and, from 1942, through the Northbrae Tunnel to The Alameda.
lines.notes: Letters were given to the lines in 1939. By 1933 the line ran to University Avenue, not Center Street; when it was extended isn't sourced, and that last stretch isn't drawn. The day of the 1933 cutback isn't sourced. The last trains ran in 1958 (HAER); April 19 or 20, 1958 is given only by later sources.

segments.name: Key Route Pier
segments.note: Ferry trains, until the Bay Bridge opened to trains
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol and fitted straight (RMS 3 m)); then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (4 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); the sheet corrected by a shift on 3 control points (Yerba Buena Island on the 1949 Oakland West sheet; +74 m E, +213 m N, RMS 44.8 m). The trestle runs straight from the shore, then curves to the ferry terminal.
segments.notes: Ferry trains ran to its end until the Bay Bridge opened to trains in January 1939; from then its land end carried the bridge trains. A 1933 fire is relayed via Wikipedia only.

segments.name: Transbay Terminal loop, San Francisco
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco North 1:24,000 (1950) (23 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). The loop as the 1950 sheet draws it ("KEY SYSTEM"): from the approach, north along the west side to the terminal's west end, through the six-track station facing Mission Street, around the east end and back south. Trains ran counter-clockwise, arriving at the station's east end.

segments.name: San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge, lower deck
segments.method: Joined to bbr-sf-loop at its start; then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco North 1:24,000 (1950) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol and fitted straight (RMS 2 m)); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (8 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (6 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). From Rincon Hill across the bridge's lower deck, through the Yerba Buena Island tunnel, to where the tracks left the bridge on its south side at the Oakland end. The 1946-50 sheets draw the bridge, not the tracks on it; the tracks were on the south half of the lower deck.

segments.name: East Bay approach and yards

lines.name: Encinal Avenue line
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's electric Red Trains across Alameda along Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue, to the Alameda Mole and its ferries; from 1939 over the Fruitvale Bridge and the Bay Bridge to San Francisco.
lines.fate_note: Replaced by Key System buses from January 18, 1941.
lines.notes: The Interurban Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific company authorized in 1936 to take over these lines (CRC D28671), ran them until 1941; the day it took over isn't sourced here. Both Alameda lines were electrified in 1911 (CRC D33732, p. 8). Not yet drawn: the track west of Webster Street to the mole, and the east end to the Fruitvale Bridge (1939–41), which the sources don't place street by street. The June 1, 1911 opening is matched to this line because the trains ran "from High street to the Alameda mole", and the Encinal Avenue line ran to High Street (CRC D33732); no source of the day names Encinal Avenue.

lines.name: Peninsula trains, San Francisco to San José
lines.summary: Trains between San Francisco and San José: the San Francisco & San Jose Railroad's from 1863, the Southern Pacific's from 1870. They left the city through the Mission, the Bernal Cut and Ocean View until the Bayshore Cutoff opened in 1907, and reached San José's Cahill Street station from the end of 1935. Caltrain runs on the same track.
lines.fate_note: On July 1, 1980 Caltrans took over the Peninsula Commute Service, with the Southern Pacific still running the trains; it became today's Caltrain (Caltrain milestones).
lines.notes: The San Francisco end moved: at 18th and Valencia Sts at first (Caltrain), the Mission (the directories), Fourth and Brannan Sts from February 14, 1864, Market and Valencia Sts by 1867, and Fourth and Townsend Sts by 1876 (Langley's directory). Only the way out of the city that the 1899 sheet draws is mapped; the earlier approaches aren't. The first train, on October 17, 1863, ran only to Big Tree Station on San Francisquito Creek; Caltrain gives regular service to Mayfield that October. In San José the trains ended at the Market Street station until 1935.

lines.name: Sacramento Northern trains, San Francisco to Bay Point and Sacramento
lines.summary: Electric trains from the Key Route pier, and from 1939 the Bay Bridge, by 40th St and Shafter Ave in Oakland, through the hills by Shepherd Canyon and the Redwood Peak tunnel, to Moraga, Walnut Creek, Concord and Bay Point, and from September 1913 on by West Pittsburg, the train ferry from Mallard to Chipps Island, Montezuma and Rio Vista Junction to Sacramento, until 1940. Drawn to the Yolo County line, where it leaves the Bay Area (decision 16).
lines.fate_note: Replaced by Pacific Greyhound buses in 1941 (CRC Decision No. 34232). Freight trains used the line through the Oakland hills until 1957.
lines.notes: The last day, June 30, 1941, rests on a railfan magazine's reminiscence of 1945; the Railroad Commission authorized the end in May 1941. Through service to Sacramento, by the Chipps Island ferry, ran from September 3, 1913 (the first through train on July 2) to on or about August 1940; after that the trains ran to Pittsburg. The Pittsburg branch itself isn't drawn yet: its opening isn't sourced.
